why_how.text: Many things lengthen your stopping distance, so a time gap gives you room to react.
Looking far ahead lets you spot hazards early and avoid last-second reactions.
Bad conditions and busy places call for a longer gap and active scanning.

scenario.text: Nico follows a car on a wet highway and wants to check his gap.

reasoning.text: Count one-thousand-one through one-thousand-three from when the car ahead passes a fixed point; reaching it before you finish means you are too close.

result.text: Nico reaches the sign at one-thousand-two, so he eases back to at least three to four seconds.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up following time with how far ahead to look.

correction.text: Following distance starts at three to four seconds and may rise to six or more, while looking ahead means scanning twenty to thirty seconds down the road.

prompt.text: It is raining hard on the freeway at high speed. What following distance should you aim for?

answer.text: Six seconds or more if needed.

rationale.text: At higher speeds or in adverse conditions, stretch your following distance to six seconds or more if needed.

narration.text: This lesson is about stopping distance and following distance. Stopping distance depends on fatigue, attention, the vehicle's type and weight, tire and brake condition, road surface and weather. Because so many things affect it, the handbook measures your safety gap in time rather than in feet. We will look at the required following distance, how to check it, when to stretch it, how to stop smoothly on wet pavement, how far ahead to look, and how to keep your eyes moving. Practice questions often mix up the following time and the look-ahead time, so we will keep them apart.

lines.text: Your car: type, weight, tires, brakes.

narration.text: Stopping distance depends on fatigue, attention, the vehicle's type and weight, tire and brake condition, road surface and weather. Some of these are about you. A tired or distracted driver reacts later. Some are about the car. A heavier vehicle, or one with worn tires or brakes, needs more distance. And some are about the road. Wet or slippery surfaces and bad weather lengthen every stop. Anticipate problems, keep a safe gap, and allow even more stopping time on poor or slippery roads. You cannot control the weather, but you can always control the space you leave ahead.

On dry or wet pavement, a following distance of three to four seconds is required. To check it, pick a fixed point, such as a sign or a shadow. When the vehicle ahead passes it, count one-thousand-one through one-thousand-three. If you reach the point before you finish counting three seconds, you are too close. A time gap works at any speed. At higher speeds you travel farther each second, so a three-second gap automatically grows longer in distance. That is why the rule is measured in seconds. Check your gap often, especially after another car moves in ahead of you.

lines.text: Stretch to six seconds or more.

narration.text: At higher speeds or in adverse conditions, stretch your following distance to six seconds or more if needed. Wet pavement needs more stopping time and space. For a smooth stop, press the brake gradually harder, and ease off just before stopping. Increase following distance at night, in bad weather, at rush hour, during lane changes and near intersections. So three to four seconds is the starting point, not the limit. Whenever conditions make stopping harder or traffic less predictable, add time. The extra seconds give you room to brake gradually instead of suddenly, which matters most on a wet road.

lines.text: Look twenty to thirty seconds ahead.
Do not stare at one thing.

narration.text: Look twenty to thirty seconds down the road to spot hazards early and avoid last-second reactions. That is much farther than your following distance. You follow three to four seconds behind, but you look twenty to thirty seconds ahead. Avoid staring at any one thing for more than a few seconds. Keep your eyes moving across the road, your mirrors and the sides of the road. Looking far ahead lets you see brake lights, merging traffic, or a hazard several cars ahead before the driver in front of you reacts, so you can slow down early and smoothly.

lines.text: Follow three to four seconds behind.
Look twenty to thirty seconds ahead.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Following distance starts at three to four seconds and may rise to six seconds or more, while looking ahead means scanning twenty to thirty seconds down the road. Options often swap these, offering twenty to thirty seconds as the following distance, or three to four seconds as how far ahead to look. Both are wrong. The small numbers belong to the gap behind the car in front of you. The big numbers belong to your view down the road. When a question asks about following, think three to four seconds. When it asks about scanning, think twenty to thirty.

Here is a quick check: it is raining hard and you are on the freeway at high speed. What following distance should you aim for? Recall the rule for adverse conditions. On dry or wet pavement, three to four seconds is required, but at higher speeds or in adverse conditions, stretch your following distance to six seconds or more if needed. Hard rain at high speed is both, so the answer is six seconds or more. Use the counting method to check it: count from when the car ahead passes a fixed point, and make sure you reach six before you get there.

To finish, stopping distance depends on fatigue, attention, the vehicle, tires and brakes, road surface and weather. On dry or wet pavement, a following distance of three to four seconds is required, and you check it by counting past a fixed point. At higher speeds or in adverse conditions, stretch it to six seconds or more. On wet pavement, brake gradually harder and ease off before stopping. Look twenty to thirty seconds ahead, keep your eyes moving, and add distance at night, in bad weather, at rush hour, during lane changes and near intersections. The hook is three to four seconds.

why_how.text: Headlights help you see and be seen, so the law sets hours and visibility rules for them.
At night you can only stop for what your headlights show, so speed must match your view.
High beams blind other drivers, so you dim them near oncoming traffic and behind others.

scenario.text: On a dark road, Jen sees headlights coming toward her about four hundred feet away while her high beams are on.

reasoning.text: Using or even flashing high beams within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle is illegal.

result.text: Jen switches to low beams right away.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking parking lights are enough in dim daylight.

correction.text: Headlights are required whenever daylight is too dim to clearly see people and vehicles at five hundred feet, and using only parking lights then is illegal.

prompt.text: An oncoming driver keeps high beams on and the glare is blinding. Where do you look?

answer.text: Toward the right edge of the road.

rationale.text: Look toward the right edge rather than into the glare, which can blind you for several seconds.

narration.text: This lesson covers headlights and night driving. Headlights do two jobs: they help you see, and they help others see you. We will look at the hours when headlights are required, when to use them in daytime, the rule about dim daylight, how fast to drive at night, when high beams are illegal, how to handle glare from oncoming drivers, and why not to use high beams behind other cars. Two of these rules share the same distance, five hundred feet, which is easy to mix up. We will put those two rules side by side so each one stays tied to its own job.

lines.text: Half hour after sunset to half hour before sunrise.
Low beams in daytime fog, rain, snow.

narration.text: Headlights must be on from one half-hour after sunset to one half-hour before sunrise, and whenever visibility is reduced. Use low beams in daytime fog, rain or snow. Turn headlights on whenever you are in doubt, since if you cannot see others, they cannot see you. Headlights are also required whenever daylight is too dim to clearly see people and vehicles at five hundred feet. Using only parking lights then is illegal. So the hours are only part of the rule. Any time the light is poor, whatever the clock says, your headlights belong on, not just your parking lights.

lines.text: Match speed to what you can see.

narration.text: At night, drive so you can stop within the distance your headlights show. If something appears at the edge of your lights, you need to be able to stop before you reach it. That means your speed should match how far you can see, not just the posted limit. On dark roads, slow down enough that the lit area ahead always covers your stopping distance. You should also dim your high beams for pedestrians and cyclists, not only for cars. A walker or rider facing your high beams can be blinded too, just as a driver can, at the moment they most need to see you.

lines.text: Illegal within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic.
Glare? Look to the right edge.

narration.text: Using, or even flashing, high beams within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle is illegal. Do not use high beams behind other vehicles either, because the glare in their mirrors distracts them. If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, look toward the right edge of the road rather than into the glare. Glare can blind you for several seconds, and it is worse through a dirty windshield. So keep your windshield clean, dim your own lights early, and if another driver does not dim theirs, guide yourself by the right edge until they pass, rather than flashing your lights back at them.

lines.text: Trap: mixing up the two rules.
Cannot see clearly at five hundred feet: lights on.
Oncoming within five hundred feet: high beams off.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Both headlight rules use five hundred feet: lights go on when you cannot see clearly at that distance, and high beams go off within that distance of oncoming traffic. Options may swap them, or use a different number such as one thousand feet. Both are wrong. The first rule is about daylight. If you cannot clearly see people and vehicles five hundred feet away, turn on your headlights, not just parking lights. The second rule is about high beams. If an oncoming vehicle is within five hundred feet, your high beams must be off, and even a quick flash is illegal.

Here is a quick check: an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, and the glare is blinding. Where do you look? Recall the glare rule. If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, look toward the right edge of the road rather than into the glare, which can blind you for several seconds and is worse through a dirty windshield. So the answer is the right edge of the road. Use it to keep your position in the lane until the other car passes. Do not flash your own high beams back, since flashing them within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle is illegal.

To finish, headlights must be on from one half-hour after sunset to one half-hour before sunrise, and whenever visibility is reduced. Use low beams in daytime fog, rain or snow, and turn lights on whenever in doubt. If you cannot clearly see people and vehicles at five hundred feet, headlights are required, and parking lights alone are illegal. At night, drive so you can stop within your headlights. Using or flashing high beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic is illegal, and you should not use them behind others. In glare, look to the right edge. The hook is five hundred feet twice.

why_how.text: A little planning and a quick check prevent breakdowns, tickets and crashes before the trip begins.
Mirrors cannot show everything, so you set them well and know where the blind spots are.
The ignition lock also locks the steering, so it must never be used while moving.

scenario.text: Before a long drive, Pat walks around the car and checks the tires and lights.

reasoning.text: Check tire inflation, damage and wear, clean windows, make sure lights and signals work, and look in front of and behind the vehicle.

result.text: Pat finds a dead taillight and replaces it before leaving.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking side mirrors show everything beside and behind the car.

correction.text: Most cars have at least two blind spots, to the left rear and right rear, that side mirrors cannot show.

prompt.text: While coasting, a driver thinks about turning the key all the way to lock to save fuel. Why must they never do that?

answer.text: The steering locks, and they lose control if they try to steer.

rationale.text: Never turn the ignition to lock while moving, because the steering locks and you lose control.

narration.text: This lesson covers what to do before you drive. A few minutes of preparation prevent many problems on the road. We will look at planning a trip, checking lights and signals, checking windows and tires, looking around the car, preventing theft, the routine before you start the engine, setting your mirrors, and one serious mistake to avoid with the ignition. Practice questions here often test blind spots and mirror setting, so we will explain those carefully. The goal is a habit you follow before every trip, so that nothing is left to chance once you pull away from the curb.

lines.text: Repairs, gas, and a shared route.
Lights and signals clean and working.

narration.text: Plan ahead: keep the vehicle in good repair, carry enough gas, and tell someone your route and expected arrival time. Make sure headlights, taillights, brake lights and turn signals are clean and working, since defective or missing equipment can get you ticketed. Clean the windshield and windows. Check tire inflation, damage and wear. And look in front of and behind the vehicle for objects, animals or people. That last step matters because a child, a pet or an object can be hidden low behind or in front of the car, right where your mirrors and windows cannot show it from the driver's seat.

lines.text: Etch the VIN on windows and parts.

narration.text: Etching the vehicle identification number on windows and main parts helps prevent theft for parts. Alarms and interlocks can discourage amateur carjackers. Before starting the engine, sit comfortably, make sure everyone is buckled, check the mirrors, and look again for anything in your path. That routine takes only seconds. Sitting comfortably means you can reach the pedals and see well. Buckling everyone before you move protects them from the first moment. Checking mirrors and looking again catches anything that moved into your path since you walked around the car.

lines.text: Two blind spots: left rear, right rear.
Inside mirror: center of the road.
Lean to set side mirrors wider.

narration.text: Most cars have at least two blind spots, to the left rear and the right rear, that side mirrors cannot show. Set the inside mirror to show the center of the road behind you. Set the outside mirrors so the vehicle's edges just show from a normal seating position. Or, for fewer blind spots, lean left to the window to set the left mirror, and lean right to the center to set the right one. Even with the best setting, a blind spot can remain. That is why a head check before changing lanes is still important. Mirrors reduce blind spots, but they never remove all of them.

Here is the trap. Many drivers believe well-set mirrors show everything around the car. That is wrong. Most cars have at least two blind spots, to the left rear and right rear, that side mirrors cannot show. Setting the outside mirrors by leaning left and right can reduce blind spots, but not remove them. Options may say that side mirrors cover the whole rear view, or that the inside mirror should be aimed at the back seat. Both are wrong. The inside mirror shows the center of the road behind you, and the side mirrors cover only part of each side.

Here is a quick check: while coasting downhill, a driver thinks about turning the key all the way to lock to save fuel. Why must they never do that? Recall the ignition rule. Never turn the ignition to lock while moving, because the steering locks and you lose control if you try to steer. So the answer is that the steering would lock. A car whose steering locks while moving cannot be turned, which can send it off the road or into other traffic. Keep the key in the run position whenever the car is moving, and turn it to lock only once you are parked.

lines.text: Never lock the ignition while moving.

narration.text: To finish, plan ahead by keeping the vehicle in good repair, carrying enough gas, and telling someone your route and arrival time. Make sure lights and signals are clean and working, since defective equipment can get you ticketed. Clean the windows, check the tires, and look in front of and behind the car. Etch the VIN to deter theft. Before starting, sit comfortably, buckle everyone, check mirrors and look again. Remember the two rear blind spots, set the inside mirror to the center of the road, and set side mirrors carefully. Never turn the ignition to lock while moving. The hook is seat, belts, mirrors, look.

why_how.text: Roadside emergencies put people on foot near traffic, which is why staying in the car is generally safest.
Locks, safe routes and parking habits reduce your risk of crime.
When threatened, your safety matters more than your car.
If you must leave a disabled vehicle, watch traffic and walk straight to a safe spot far from the road.

scenario.text: Lou's car breaks down on a busy highway at night.

reasoning.text: Pull as far off the traveled road as possible, turn on the four-way flashers, and stay inside buckled up.

result.text: Lou pulls far onto the shoulder, turns on the flashers, stays buckled and calls for help.

claim.text: Common mistake: getting out to change a flat tire on a dark roadside.

correction.text: With a flat tire, do not get out to fix it; drive slowly to a well-lit service station or store lot and phone for help.

prompt.text: Your disabled car is in a dangerous spot and you must leave it. How should you go?

answer.text: Watch traffic and walk straight to a safe spot far from the road.

rationale.text: If you must leave a disabled vehicle, watch traffic and walk straight to a safe spot far from the road, since walking on a freeway is dangerous and illegal.

narration.text: This lesson covers your personal safety when things go wrong or when you are in a risky place. From two thousand fourteen to two thousand eighteen, about ten percent of pedestrian traffic deaths involved a roadside emergency, which shows how dangerous it is to be on foot beside traffic. We will look at what to do in a roadside emergency, how to reduce the risk of crime while driving and parking, what to do with a flat tire, how to respond to a suspicious person or a carjacker, and how to handle a breakdown. The safest choice is often to stay in your car.

lines.text: About ten percent of pedestrian deaths.

narration.text: From two thousand fourteen to two thousand eighteen, about ten percent of pedestrian traffic deaths involved a roadside emergency. In a roadside emergency, the safest choice is generally to stay in the car with your seat belt buckled until help arrives. That may feel strange, since many people want to get out and look at the problem. But standing beside a car on a busy road puts you right next to fast traffic. Inside the car, buckled, you have the car's protection around you. So unless staying put is clearly unsafe, remain in your seat and call for help.

Keep doors and windows locked. Prefer freeways over streets through high-crime areas, and know where help, such as a police station or an open business, is nearby. Neither hitchhike nor give rides to hitchhikers. Keep keys out of the parked car and its ignition, and shut the sunroof at night and in risky areas. When parking, choose the safest route, park close to your destination, have keys ready when returning, and check inside the car for intruders before getting in. These habits are simple, and together they make you a much harder target for anyone looking for an easy chance.

lines.text: Flat tire: drive slowly to a lit place.
Suspicious person: drive away or honk.

narration.text: With a flat tire, do not get out to fix it. Drive slowly to a well-lit service station or store lot and phone for help. If someone suspicious approaches your car, drive away or sound the horn. Stay inside with doors locked, and call for help by mobile phone, which Michigan law allows for emergencies. If a carjacker wants your vehicle, give it up without a fight. Stay calm, and note a good description to give the police. A car can be replaced. You cannot. In each of these cases, the advice puts your personal safety ahead of the vehicle and its tires.

If your car breaks down, pull as far off the traveled road as possible, turn on the four-way flashers, and stay inside buckled up. The handbook recommends that a trained, equipped professional assist with the vehicle. If you must leave a disabled vehicle, watch traffic and walk straight to a safe spot far from the road, since walking on a freeway is dangerous and illegal. So the first choice is to stay in the car. Leaving is the exception, used only when staying is unsafe, and even then you move straight away from traffic rather than walking along the roadside.

lines.text: Trap: get out and fix the problem.
Flat tire: drive to a lit place.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a tire goes flat or the car breaks down, many drivers get out to fix it right there. That is usually wrong. With a flat tire, do not get out to fix it. Drive slowly to a well-lit service station or store lot and phone for help. If your car breaks down, pull as far off the road as possible, turn on the four-way flashers, and stay inside buckled up. Options may suggest changing the tire on a dark shoulder, or standing behind the car to wave at traffic. Both put you on foot beside moving traffic, which is the danger the rules avoid.

lines.text: Disabled car in a bad spot.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: your disabled car is in a dangerous spot, and you decide you must leave it. How should you go? Recall the rule for leaving a disabled vehicle. If you must leave it, watch traffic and walk straight to a safe spot far from the road, since walking on a freeway is dangerous and illegal. So the answer is to check traffic and move directly away from the road to safety. Do not walk along the freeway shoulder toward an exit, and do not cross lanes. Once you are safely away, call for help and wait there.

To finish, about ten percent of pedestrian traffic deaths from two thousand fourteen to two thousand eighteen involved a roadside emergency, and the safest choice is generally to stay in the car buckled until help arrives. Keep doors and windows locked, prefer freeways through high-crime areas, never hitchhike or pick up hitchhikers, and check your car before getting in. With a flat tire, drive slowly to a well-lit place. Drive away or honk if someone suspicious approaches, and give up your car to a carjacker. In a breakdown, pull far off, use flashers and stay inside, and if you must leave, walk straight to safety. The hook is stay in, stay buckled.

why_how.text: The law requires you to stay at a crash and help the injured.
Moving drivable cars off the main road prevents a second crash.
Exchanging information and notifying police in serious crashes make sure the crash is handled properly.

scenario.text: After a fender-bender with no injuries, both cars can still be driven safely.

reasoning.text: If no one is seriously hurt or killed and the vehicle can be driven safely, a licensed driver or passenger must move it off the main road.

result.text: The drivers move both cars to a nearby parking lot and exchange information there.

claim.text: Common mistake: leaving crashed cars in the lane until police arrive, even when they can be driven safely.

correction.text: If no one is seriously hurt and the vehicle can be driven safely, move it off the main road to a safe spot such as the shoulder, median or a parking lot.

prompt.text: A crash causes about two thousand dollars in damage but no injuries. Must police be notified?

answer.text: Yes. The damage is more than one thousand dollars.

rationale.text: Notify police when a crash causes injuries or more than one thousand dollars in property damage.

narration.text: This lesson covers what to do after a crash. The law sets clear duties, and knowing them ahead of time helps you stay calm when it happens. We will look at why you must never leave the scene, getting medical aid for anyone hurt, when to move the vehicles off the road, what information to exchange, and when police must be notified. Practice questions often test the police notification threshold and the rule about moving cars, so we will look at how those two rules work together. The short version is to stay, help, clear the road when it is safe, exchange information and report.

Leaving the scene of a crash you are involved in is illegal, and it can bring fines, jail or both, with heavier penalties if alcohol, injuries or deaths are involved. After a crash, help get medical aid for anyone injured. So your first duties are to stay and to make sure anyone who is hurt gets help. Even a minor crash creates these duties. Driving away because the damage looks small, or because you are in a hurry, is still leaving the scene. Stop, check on everyone involved, and call for medical help if anyone is hurt, before you deal with the cars.

lines.text: No serious injury and drivable: move it.

narration.text: If no one is seriously hurt or killed, and the vehicle can be driven safely, a licensed driver or passenger must move it off the main road to a safe spot, such as the shoulder, the median or a nearby parking lot. Then exchange names, addresses, license numbers, registration and insurance information with the other drivers. Moving the cars prevents a second crash, because cars stopped in a travel lane are easy to hit. It also lets traffic keep moving. Once the cars are in a safe spot, take your time exchanging the full set of information with everyone involved.

lines.text: Or more than one thousand dollars damage.

narration.text: Notify police when a crash causes injuries, or more than one thousand dollars in property damage. Police must be notified in those cases, and a drivable vehicle in a crash without serious injury or death must still be moved off the main road when safe. So reporting and moving are separate duties. A crash can require both. Moving the car out of traffic does not cancel the duty to notify police if the damage is over the threshold. And waiting for police does not mean leaving a drivable car in the lane. Do both: clear the road, then report as required.

lines.text: Trap: leave cars until police come.
Drivable and no serious injury: move.
Report injuries or big damage too.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think they must leave crashed cars exactly where they stopped until police arrive. That is wrong when no one is seriously hurt and the cars can be driven safely. Then a licensed driver or passenger must move the vehicle off the main road to a safe spot. Options may say moving the cars destroys evidence, or that the police threshold means you never have to move them. Both are wrong. Police must be notified when a crash causes any injury or more than one thousand dollars in damage, and a drivable car must still be moved when safe.

Here is a quick check: a crash causes about two thousand dollars in damage but no injuries. Must police be notified? Recall the threshold. Notify police when a crash causes injuries or more than one thousand dollars in property damage. Two thousand dollars is more than one thousand, so the answer is yes, even though no one was hurt. If the cars can be driven safely, move them off the main road first, exchange information with the other driver, and then notify police. The threshold is about damage, not only about injuries.

To finish, leaving the scene of a crash you are involved in is illegal and can bring fines, jail or both, with heavier penalties if alcohol, injuries or deaths are involved. Help get medical aid for anyone injured. If no one is seriously hurt and the vehicle can be driven safely, move it off the main road to a safe spot such as the shoulder, median or a parking lot. Exchange names, addresses, license numbers, registration and insurance information. Notify police when a crash causes injuries or more than one thousand dollars in damage. The hook is never leave a crash.

why_how.text: Deer crashes are common and costly in Michigan, so every driver should know how to avoid and handle them.
Deer are most active in certain seasons and times and travel in groups, so you adjust when and where you watch.
Swerving to avoid a deer can be worse than hitting it, so the rule is to brake and stay in your lane.
A deer crash is reported to local police, the sheriff, state police or the DNR, who can issue a permit to keep the deer.

scenario.text: At dusk in October, Ellie sees a deer cross the road ahead.

reasoning.text: Be especially alert in fall and spring and at dawn and dusk; if you see one deer, slow down, because deer usually travel in groups.

result.text: Ellie slows down, and a second deer crosses a moment later.

claim.text: Myth: a deer whistle or honking will keep deer off the road.

correction.text: Deer whistles, flashing high beams and honking do not keep deer away.

prompt.text: You hit a deer and it is killed. Whom can you report it to, and can you keep it?

answer.text: Local police, the sheriff, state police or the DNR, who can issue a permit to keep the deer.

rationale.text: Report a deer crash to local police, the county sheriff, Michigan State Police or the Department of Natural Resources, who can issue a permit to keep the deer.

lines.text: What to do if a hit is coming.

narration.text: This lesson covers deer crashes, a serious problem on Michigan roads. Michigan has about sixty thousand vehicle-deer crashes a year, and officials suspect up to half go unreported. We will look at what these crashes cost, how to report one, how to avoid deer, when to be most alert, why one deer usually means more, which popular tricks do not work, and what to do if hitting a deer cannot be avoided. Practice questions often test the last point, because the instinct to swerve is strong and wrong. We will make the correct response clear and explain the reasoning behind it.

lines.text: About sixty thousand crashes a year.
Average damage two thousand one hundred dollars.

narration.text: Michigan has about sixty thousand vehicle-deer crashes a year, and officials suspect up to half go unreported. The average deer crash causes two thousand one hundred dollars in damage, usually to the front end. Statewide costs are estimated at one hundred thirty million dollars a year. Report a deer crash to local police, the county sheriff, Michigan State Police, or the Department of Natural Resources, who can issue a permit to keep the deer. So deer crashes are not rare events. Any driver on rural or suburban roads should expect to meet deer, and should know how to respond when it happens.

lines.text: Seat belt on; watch for signs.

narration.text: To avoid deer, stay aware, awake, alert and sober, always wear a seat belt, and watch for deer crossing signs. Be especially alert in fall and spring, and at dawn and dusk, though deer crashes happen year-round. If you see one deer, slow down, because deer usually travel in groups. So timing and place matter. A deer crossing sign marks an area where deer are known to cross. Dawn and dusk are when deer are most active and when light is poor. And when one deer appears, assume others are close behind it, and slow down before they step out.

lines.text: Whistles, high beams, honking: no effect.

narration.text: Deer whistles, flashing high beams and honking do not keep deer away. So do not rely on them. If hitting a deer is unavoidable, do not swerve. Stay in your lane, brake firmly, grip the wheel with both hands, and come to a controlled stop. Then steer well off the road. Gripping the wheel with both hands keeps the car straight as you brake. Staying in your lane and stopping under control is the response the handbook gives, and your seat belt, which you should always wear, protects you if the hit comes. Slow, straight and steady is the plan.

lines.text: Trap: swerve to miss the deer.
Stay in your lane and brake.
Whistles and honking do not work.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a deer jumps in front of the car, the instinct is to swerve. That is wrong. If hitting a deer is unavoidable, do not swerve: stay in your lane, brake firmly, grip the wheel with both hands, come to a controlled stop, and steer well off the road. A second trap is trusting gadgets. Deer whistles, flashing high beams and honking do not keep deer away. Options may suggest a whistle on the bumper as the best protection. The real protection is staying alert, wearing your seat belt, and slowing down when you see deer or deer crossing signs.

lines.text: Can you report it and keep it?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you hit a deer, and it is killed. Whom can you report it to, and can you keep it? Recall the reporting rule. Report a deer crash to local police, the county sheriff, Michigan State Police or the Department of Natural Resources, who can issue a permit to keep the deer. So the answer is any of those agencies, and they can issue a permit if you want to keep the deer. Reporting also matters because officials suspect up to half of all deer crashes go unreported. So reporting is the step many drivers skip, and it is one you should not.

To finish, Michigan has about sixty thousand vehicle-deer crashes a year, with up to half unreported. The average deer crash causes two thousand one hundred dollars in damage, usually to the front end. Report a deer crash to police, the sheriff, state police or the DNR, who can issue a permit to keep the deer. Stay aware, awake, alert and sober, wear your seat belt, and watch for crossing signs, especially in fall, spring, dawn and dusk. One deer means more. Whistles, flashing and honking do not work. If a hit is unavoidable, brake firmly and stay in your lane. The hook is brake, don't swerve.

why_how.text: Calm, predictable actions during a traffic stop keep both you and the officer safe.
Disputes belong in court, not at the roadside.
An officer's directions take priority over signals and signs.

scenario.text: Flashing lights appear behind Ari on a city street at night.

reasoning.text: Pull off to the right as soon as it is safe and stop; stay in the car buckled, turn on the interior light, open the window and keep empty hands on the wheel.

result.text: Ari pulls right, stops, turns on the dome light and waits with hands on the wheel.

claim.text: Common mistake: reaching for your license before the officer asks.

correction.text: Take out your license, registration and insurance card only when asked, and tell the officer where they are first.

prompt.text: An officer at an intersection waves you through while your light is red. What do you do?

rationale.text: An officer's directions take priority over other traffic control devices.

narration.text: This lesson covers traffic stops and officer directions. Being pulled over can feel stressful, but knowing what to expect makes it go smoothly and safely for everyone. We will look at how to pull over, what to do once you are stopped, when to reach for your documents, how to handle a disagreement about a ticket or the officer's conduct, and why an officer's directions come before traffic signals. The theme of the lesson is calm, predictable behavior. Sudden movements and arguments make a stop harder for everyone, while clear and simple actions keep it short.

lines.text: Pull right as soon as it is safe.
Stay buckled; interior light after dusk.
Window open, empty hands on the wheel.

narration.text: When an officer signals you to pull over, pull off to the right as soon as it is safe and stop. Stay calm, and follow orders without making movements that could escalate things. During the stop, stay in the car with your seat belt buckled. Turn on the interior lights after dusk, open the window, and keep empty hands on the wheel. Ask your passengers to stay quiet, with their hands visible. Each of these steps lets the officer see that everyone in the car is calm and that no one is reaching for anything, which helps the stop stay routine and brief.

lines.text: Argue in court, not at roadside.

narration.text: Take out your license, registration and insurance card only when asked, and tell the officer where they are first. That way, reaching into a pocket or the glove box is expected rather than surprising. Do not argue about the stop or a ticket. Take a ticket dispute to the court. And report officer conduct you think was inappropriate to the officer's supervisor. So there is a proper place for every disagreement, and the roadside is not it. Accept the ticket calmly, and if you believe it is wrong, you will have your chance to explain in court.

lines.text: Trap: have documents ready in hand.
Tell the officer where they are.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think it is helpful to dig out their license and registration before the officer reaches the car. That is wrong. Take out your license, registration and insurance card only when asked, and tell the officer where they are first. Until then, keep empty hands on the wheel. Options may suggest getting out of the car to meet the officer, or reaching into the glove box right away. Both are wrong. Stay in the car, buckled, with your hands visible. Moving only when asked, and saying what you are reaching for, keeps the stop calm.

Here is a quick check: at an intersection, your light is red, but an officer directing traffic waves you through. What do you do? Recall the rule about officer directions. An officer's directions take priority over other traffic control devices. So the answer is to follow the officer and go when waved through, carefully. The officer's signal overrides the light, even when the two do not match. When an officer is directing traffic, watch the officer rather than the light, and do what the officer signals. Calm and simple wins.

To finish, when an officer signals you to pull over, pull off to the right as soon as it is safe and stop, stay calm, and follow orders without sudden movements. Stay in the car buckled, turn on interior lights after dusk, open the window, and keep empty hands on the wheel, with passengers quiet and hands visible. Take out your license, registration and insurance card only when asked, after saying where they are. Do not argue; take ticket disputes to court and report conduct concerns to a supervisor. An officer's directions take priority over other traffic controls. The hook is hands on the wheel.
